Hypocnemis, a species complex of warbling antbirds from the passerine family Thamnophilidae. Found throughout the Amazon Rainforest in South America, this group of passerines consists of six species of antbird in the genus Hypocnemis. Until 2007, the complex was originally considered a single species, but multiple species are now differentiated by their vocalizations, differences in plumage, and habitat.

Evolutionary background
The Amazon River and its tributaries (such as the Rio Negro and the Rio Branco) are boundaries to warbling antbird distribution. These geographical boundaries are thought to have contributed to species differentiation that occurred less than 2 million years ago. Range overlaps between H. striata and H. ochrogyna have been found to result in hybridization, but high linkage disequlibrium maintains genetic differentiation, despite the plumage and calls of different species being extremely similar. Because species ranges of this genus exist in allopatry, differentiation in habitat occupation likely also maintains genetic differentiation. Physical traits such as beak length and width, tarsus length and width, retrices, and total length vary between species.
Voice
}}
Warbling antbirds have a complex set of vocalizations, which include male songs,  female songs, and common calls (used by both sexes), chirrs, and chit calls. The identification of multiple species within the complex relies heavily on vocalizations, with most species pairs found to differ in both songs and common calls. Researchers speculate that common calls distinct to specific species pairs might be involved in mate selection.
Sexual Dimorphism
The plumage of male and female individuals is not remarkably distinct. Some physical traits vary between the sexes, including beak height, tarsus length and head length. Females of the species Hypocnemis peruviana weigh more than males by an average margin of 0.45 grams.
Behavior
Nesting
The warbling antbird nests on the branches of low shrubs or trees, typically  from the ground. At this height, the nest site can be covered by dense vegetation. The nest is attached to a forked branch at two points, and foliage provides a roof for the nest and hides it from view, giving the birds reduced risk of nest predation. The nest is cup-shaped, usually woven from twigs, leaves, moss, plant fibers, and other available materials. The antbirds usually line the inside of the nest with soft items, such as feathers or fine grass.
Nesting is mainly carried out by females, although males may assist in collecting materials or guarding the surrounding area. The nesting period ranges in length from a few days to a week.
Warbling antbirds begin to breed in the rainy season, when food sources are abundant. The incubation period is about 14-16 days, and the chicks are fed by both parents. Both parents participate in caring for offspring. In addition, they use environmental concealment to avoid predators and drive away potential threats near the nest by singing or feigning.
Foraging
The warbling antbird usually appears in pairs when foraging, performing territorial duets. These calls serve to establish and maintain territory, helping to prevent intrusion by other individuals. The calls also help maintain contact between mates, ensuring that they are aware of each other's location.
Warbling antbirds display a foraging strategy in which they follow the trails of ant colonies, helping them find food more efficiently, as the ants drive out invertebrate prey such as other insects and spiders. This foraging technique is mainly used during the day, especially in the early morning and evening, when insect activity is highest. Warbling antbirds have a diverse diet that varies with season and habitat.
Conservation status
According to the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), five of the species are assessed as Least Concern (LC). The Rondonia warbling antbird (H. ochrogyna) is assessed as Vulnerable (VU).
